newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila shares savaged as correction continues.
newsitem.headline: Manila shares savaged as correction continues.

text.p: Philippine shares, one of the brightest boys on the block a few months ago, looked far from dazzling after Tuesday's savaging dragged the market to its lowest in over two years.

In almost vertical decline since hitting a record high in early February, prices have been knocked by a combination of disenchantment with the region, rising U.S. interest rates and deep concerns about local banks and property companies.
"We are seeing end-of-cycle delirium. This is the first phase of the correction," said SBC Warburg analyst Joey Salceda.
"The cleansing process has just started. There is too much froth."
After the biggest one-day fall in two years on Tuesday, the index was sitting about 20 percent below its February peak.
"This has been a savage sell-down. The bottom line is that we are being de-rated with the rest of the region," an analyst with one foreign investment bank said.
Many investors are increasingly worried the Philippines may be on the verge of emulating the Thai land and banking crisis.
The Central Bank said on Tuesday it had set a 20 percent limit on loan exposure of banks to the real estate sector, the first time it has made such a move.
An estimated two-thirds of the Manila market is in the hands of foreign investors and some analysts doubted that this price slump would entice many back.
"We don't see any natural bottom-fishing from foreign funds in general because a lot are overweight already," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's senior associate director of research, Tien Doe.
"Concerns (about property and banks) are long term and will take a while to work out," he added.
Investors now have a nail-biting wait for more first-quarter corporate results.
Numbers have so far given little encouragement, most coming in either at or below target.
"Dismal earnings are not just in the property sector. There could be more. If limited to property and banks, that's fine but not if it spreads," one analyst said.
SBC Warburg's Salceda said he was targeting 2,400 as the time to return to the market. The index finished at just over 2,700 on Tuesday.
"I think 2,400 is a fair re-entry point. It's not so steep as Thailand," he said of the Bangkok market drop, which ended what analysts said had become an unsustainable boom.
"Thailand's market had eight years of booze. We've had three years of social drinking, so the hangover is limited," he added.
Chris Hunt, head of reasearch at WI Carr in Manila, said he was not all that concerned by the latest drop, which represented a much needed shake-out.
"There's a real possibility of buying returning. We could see the market turn around."
Hunt pointed to a fundamentally solid economy that was growing steadily.
Luz Lorenzo, economist at Peregrine Securities, refused to be bowed by the slump, seeing buying chances in top quality shares, even in the banking and property sectors.
"It is hard to go against very negative sentiment but I feel it is just sentiment. Blue chips really do have value," she said.
